claims.text: Moderate- or low-temperature reduction of a solid, mixed-metal precursor limits precursor or atomic mobility.
Limited atomic mobility forces the reduction to be rapid.
The constituent noble-metal precursors reduce sequentially.
Restricted mobility kinetically freezes a largely random alloy configuration during particle formation.
Adding more element types innately promotes a more random nanoparticle configuration.
The combination of high element count and inhibited mobility favors formation of a single-phase high-entropy alloy nanoparticle in a five-noble-metal precursor system.
Binary mixtures under comparable restricted-mobility conditions are more prone to phase separation than five-element mixtures.
The solid single-source precursor contains noble-metal ions in near-equimolar ratios.
A solution-based process can provide the same diffusion-constrained environment as reduction of a solid mixed precursor.
Stronger pairwise interactions in binary systems promote phase segregation.
Combinatorial mixing in quinary systems can offset element-specific miscibility preferences.
Quinary nanoparticles produced under the proposed conditions will be uniformly alloyed and single-phase.
Binary nanoparticles produced under identical low-mobility conditions will exhibit phase segregation or ordered domains.
Five-component nanoparticles are not invariably homogeneous because unfavorable binary mixing enthalpies can still cause elemental segregation.
The low-temperature formation principle may be transferable to other syntheses using similar solid, mixed precursors.
The proposed mechanism may cease to govern at high temperatures because increased atomic mobility permits equilibration.
A homogeneous single-phase binary product, or failure of the quinary material to become single-phase under the controlled conditions, would falsify the proposed element-count-plus-mobility mechanism.

contradictions.description: The initial state and boundary restrict the hypothesis to a solid, mixed-metal precursor, but the intervention also presents a solution-based process as an equivalent example. Dissolved species do not necessarily have the restricted mobility central to the stated solid-precursor mechanism.
